pages.text: The Jungle Book

image.note: Cover: a boy among wolves in moonlit jungle

pages.text: Contents. The Man-Cub / The Law of the Jungle / Shere Khan's Shadow / Stolen by the Monkeys / The Red Flower / The Council Rock.

Deep in the jungles of India, where the trees grow thick and the night is full of eyes, the animals keep an old and solemn Law. This is the story of a boy who came to live among them, and of the tiger who swore to hunt him down.

image.note: Moonlit jungle, glowing eyes in the dark

pages.text: It was warm evening when Father Wolf woke to hunt. But as he stretched, a small shadow came stumbling into the mouth of the cave: not a fawn, not a cub, but a naked brown baby, who could barely walk, looking up and laughing.

image.note: Baby crawling into a wolf's cave

pages.text: "A man's cub," whispered Mother Wolf, her eyes soft. "How little he is. How bold." The baby pushed in among the wolf cubs, warm against her side, quite unafraid. "See, he takes his supper with the rest. Would you turn him out, then?"

image.note: Baby nestled among wolf cubs

pages.text: Just then a great striped head filled the cave mouth, and a voice like thunder rolled in. It was Shere Khan the tiger, lame in one foot and cruel in temper. "The cub is mine," he growled. "His people are near. Give him to me."

image.note: Shere Khan's striped head at the cave mouth

pages.text: But the cave was too narrow for a tiger, and Mother Wolf stood over the child with every hair on end. "The man's cub is mine, Lame One," she said. "He shall live and run with the pack. Now go." And Shere Khan, who could not reach them, backed away, snarling promises of revenge.

image.note: Mother Wolf defiant, tiger retreating

pages.text: So the boy was named Mowgli, the little frog, and taken to the Council Rock, where the whole pack meets under the moon to look at their new cubs. There the Law says a man-cub may join, if two who are not his parents will speak for him.

image.note: Wolf pack gathered at Council Rock under the moon

pages.text: Two spoke. Baloo the sleepy brown bear, who teaches the cubs the Law, rumbled, "Let the man-cub run with us." And Bagheera the black panther, sleek and clever, said, "I too speak for him," and paid the price of a fresh-killed bull. And so Mowgli became a wolf of the pack.

image.note: Baloo and Bagheera speaking at the Rock

pages.text: The years passed, and Mowgli grew. He ran with his wolf brothers, and pulled thorns from their feet, and learned the ways of the jungle as no man ever had. To him the wolves were family, the jungle was home, and he feared nothing that walked or crawled or flew.

image.note: Older Mowgli running with young wolves

pages.text: Only Bagheera, watching, would sometimes sigh. "Little Frog," the panther told him, "you are of the jungle, and yet you are not. One day the pack may turn, for men and wolves do not stay friends for ever. Remember then that Bagheera loves you." Mowgli only laughed. He did not yet understand.

image.note: Bagheera speaking seriously to Mowgli

pages.text: Every young thing in the jungle must learn the Law, and Mowgli learned it from Baloo. The Law is old and wise: hunt for food and never for fun, let the small ones grow, keep the peace at the drinking-places, and know the Master Words that keep you safe.

image.note: Baloo teaching Mowgli, paw raised

pages.text: "Say the Master Word of the Hunting-People," Baloo would growl, and Mowgli would call it, and every wolf and jackal would answer. "Now the Word of the Birds," and Mowgli would whistle it, and the kite far above would dip its wing. "Now the Word of the Snake-People," and Mowgli would hiss it true.

image.note: Mowgli calling; birds and animals answering

pages.text: "With these words," said Baloo, "no one in the jungle will harm you, for you have said: we are of one blood, you and I. Learn them well, Little Frog. A day may come when they save your life." Mowgli grumbled at the endless lessons, but he learned.

image.note: Mowgli reluctantly reciting, Baloo patient

pages.text: Bagheera taught him too, but different things: how to move without a sound, how to climb, how to look and truly see. "Baloo teaches you the Law," said the panther. "I teach you to stay alive. Both you will need, for the Lame Tiger has not forgotten you."

image.note: Bagheera teaching Mowgli to move silently

pages.text: And it was true. Wherever Mowgli went, he felt the tiger watching from the long grass. Shere Khan could not take him while the pack was strong. But the tiger was patient, and he had begun to whisper to the younger wolves that a man had no place among them.

image.note: Shere Khan whispering to young wolves in the grass

pages.text: As the old pack leader grew grey and weak, Shere Khan's whispers spread like a sickness. "Why do we, the free people, take orders from a man's cub?" the young wolves began to mutter. "He is not one of us. Look how he stares. We cannot meet his eyes."

image.note: Young wolves muttering, uneasy

pages.text: For that was the strange thing: no animal in the jungle could look Mowgli in the eyes for long. When he stared, they turned away, and it made them afraid, though they did not know why. Only Mowgli did not know his own power.

image.note: Mowgli's steady gaze; a wolf looking away

pages.text: Bagheera came to him one evening, grave. "It is coming, Little Frog, as I said it would. The old leader is failing. When he can no longer keep his place, the pack will meet, and Shere Khan means to turn them against you. You must be ready."

image.note: Bagheera warning Mowgli at dusk

pages.text: "But they are my brothers," said Mowgli, hurt. "Brothers," said Bagheera softly, "can forget. There is one thing in the whole jungle that even Shere Khan fears, one thing that can keep you safe. Do you know what it is?" Mowgli shook his head. "The Red Flower," said the panther.

image.note: Mowgli puzzled; Bagheera solemn

pages.text: "The Red Flower?" "That is the jungle's name for it, for we dare not speak its true name. It grows in the huts of men, in pots, warm and bright and hungry. Every beast, even the tiger, even I, runs from it. Fetch some, and keep it close, against the night the pack turns."

image.note: Distant village huts glowing with firelight

pages.text: But before that night came, another danger found Mowgli first. The Monkey-People, the chattering Bandar-log who swing through the treetops with no Law and no leader, had been watching the clever man-cub, and they wanted him for their own.

image.note: Monkeys watching Mowgli from the branches

pages.text: One hot afternoon, while Baloo dozed, a hundred hairy hands seized Mowgli and swept him up into the treetops, swinging him away over the jungle roof faster than any man could run below. "Baloo! Bagheera!" he cried, but the branches carried him far.

image.note: Monkeys carrying Mowgli through the treetops

pages.text: As he was whisked along, Mowgli remembered his lessons. High above flew Chil the kite, and Mowgli called the Master Word of the Birds. "We be of one blood, you and I! Mark my trail, and tell Baloo and Bagheera where I am taken!" The kite dipped its wing and wheeled away with the message.

image.note: Mowgli calling up to the kite

pages.text: The monkeys carried him to the Cold Lairs, an old ruined city swallowed by the jungle, all broken walls and empty halls. There they set him down and danced around him, shrieking, "You are wise, be our leader, tell us what to do!" But being monkeys, none of them ever listened for the answer.

image.note: Ruined city, monkeys dancing around Mowgli

pages.text: Meanwhile Baloo and Bagheera raced to the rescue, and with them came the most feared hunter of all: Kaa, the great rock python, long and patient and old, who had a score to settle with the thieving monkeys.

image.note: Kaa the python gliding through the jungle

pages.text: When they reached the Cold Lairs the monkeys swarmed, and even brave Bagheera was nearly overwhelmed. Then Kaa came. He did not hurry. He began, slowly, to sway, and to speak in a low humming voice, and the monkeys froze where they stood, unable to look away.

image.note: Kaa swaying, monkeys frozen and staring

pages.text: In the confusion Bagheera called, "Mowgli, the water! Jump into the water!" and Mowgli dived into an old stone tank, safe from the spell that held the monkeys. Baloo and Bagheera bounded to him, and together they slipped away into the night, leaving the Bandar-log to Kaa.

image.note: Mowgli leaping into water, friends beside him

pages.text: That night, sore and shaken, Mowgli understood at last why Bagheera worried. The jungle was wide and full of dangers, and cleverness alone was not enough. "I should have listened," he said. "Now," said Bagheera gently, "you begin to be wise."

image.note: Mowgli resting, Baloo and Bagheera near

pages.text: The night the pack turned came sooner than they feared. Word ran through the jungle: the old leader had fallen, and Shere Khan walked openly now, the young wolves at his heels. "Tonight," said Bagheera. "Fetch the Red Flower, Little Frog. Tonight you will need it."

image.note: Bagheera urgent; wolves gathering far off

pages.text: So Mowgli crept down to the village at the jungle's edge, where he had seen the huts glow. Through a window he watched a woman feed a small clay pot with sticks, and saw the Red Flower leap up, bright and warm. When morning came, he traded a boy for a pot of glowing embers and carried it away, guarding it like treasure.

image.note: Mowgli carrying a glowing fire-pot from the village

pages.text: All day he fed it dry branches, as he had seen the woman do, and watched it grow and dance. "So this is the thing the whole jungle fears," he thought. "This little dancing flower. Even the tiger." And he was no longer quite so afraid of the night ahead.

image.note: Mowgli feeding the fire-pot, flames dancing

pages.text: That evening the pack met at the Council Rock, and the air was wrong. The young wolves would not meet his eye. Shere Khan lay at the edge, huge and confident. "The man-cub has no place here," the tiger rumbled. "Give him to me." And this time, many of the young wolves growled agreement.

image.note: Tense Council Rock, Shere Khan confident

pages.text: Mowgli stood, and in his hand was the fire-pot, though the wolves did not yet know it. "You call me man-cub," he said, and his voice was steady. "Very well. Since you will not have me as a brother, I will be a man, as you say." And he thrust a dry branch into the pot, and drew it out crowned with the Red Flower.

image.note: Mowgli holding up a blazing branch

pages.text: The whole pack leapt back, crying out in terror, for there is nothing in all the jungle that does not fear fire. Mowgli walked to the great tiger and struck the ground before him with the flaming branch, and Shere Khan cowered, snarling, singed and shamed.

image.note: Shere Khan cowering from the flaming branch

pages.text: "Go," said Mowgli. "Go, Lame One, and do not come back. The next time we meet at the Council Rock, it will not go well for you." And Shere Khan slunk away into the dark, beaten, while the pack watched in silence. But Mowgli's heart was heavy, not glad.

image.note: Shere Khan slinking away; Mowgli watching

pages.text: For as he stood there, master of the moment, Mowgli felt hot drops on his face, the first he had ever known, and did not understand them. "What is this, Bagheera?" he asked. "Am I hurt?" "No, Little Frog," said the panther gently. "These are only tears, such as men use. Now I know you are a man, and a man's cub no longer."

image.note: Mowgli's first tears; Bagheera beside him

pages.text: So Mowgli's time among the wolves came to its turning. He would go down, one day, to the huts of men, to learn at last what he was. But not yet. "The jungle is mine tonight," he said, wiping his eyes, "and the Red Flower is mine, and Shere Khan is beaten. Tomorrow can wait." And he ran off into the dark with his wolf brothers.

image.note: Mowgli running into the jungle with wolves, fire glowing

pages.text: The Law of the Jungle, that Baloo taught. Hunt only for food. Keep peace at the water. Let the young grow. Say the Master Words, for we are all of one blood. And remember: the strong protect the small, or they are not truly strong at all.

image.note: The jungle at peace, animals at the waterhole

pages.text: Mowgli's story goes on: how he lived among men, and returned, and kept his promise about the tiger. But that is a tale for another book. For now the moon is up, the pack is running, and somewhere a boy laughs in the dark, at home between two worlds.

image.note: Full moon over the jungle, running shapes
